new_statements.quote: Word stress is lexically contrastive in Iñapari. (16) Lexical stress contrasts: anáʋa 'they', anaʋá 'canoe'; ʔuʔá 'nest', ʔúʔa 'woodpecker'; háma 'to hear', hamá 'tapir'. Stress overwhelmingly occurs on the penultimate syllable in many elicited lexical items in my data. Consequently, I only indicate stress if it is not on the penultimate syllable. Acoustically, word stress appears to be associated with changes in intensity (and perhaps also pitch). ... Firstly, stress change can be used for polarity question intonation, in which case it always occurs on the final syllable, no matter where it occurs lexically. ... Secondly, some bound morphemes have fixed stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: For Iñapari (the language Glottolog files this wordlist): stress is lexically specified and can contrast (minimal pairs), but the default and overwhelmingly most frequent position is the penultimate syllable; Parker 1995 (sec. 4, pp. 17-18) describes the same system as a pitch accent with one high tone per word whose position is 'mayormente impredecible', rarely word-initial except in some disyllables. Nothing whatsoever is stated about stress for the 25-word Pacahuaras/Pacaguara-Mercier list itself.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described (Parker 1995 notes a few words with two high tones, e.g. [iwáná] 'río').
new_statements.exceptions: Polar-question intonation moves stress to the word-final syllable regardless of lexical position (Rogers treats this as sentential); some bound morphemes (causative -ʔá) attract primary stress; a separate morpheme-bound high tone (-yíí contrastive focus, tʃií 'earth') co-occurs with stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern modern Iñapari of the Río Piedras, Peru (elicited lexical items and inflected words), not the extinct 1880s Pacaguara-Mercier/Pacahuaras vocabulary; applicability to paca1243 rests solely on Hammarström's equation 'Pacahuaras = Pacaguara-Mercier = Iñapari [inp]'.
new_statements.identity_note: paca1243 'Pacahuaras-Castillo' is not an independent language: Glottolog 5.1 carried it as Unclassifiable with zero references, and the Glottolog GitHub master retired it to Bookkeeping on 2026-08-23 (commit 8fdbc6f1, PR #1386). Hammarström's annotation of del Castillo 1929 reads 'Pacahuaras = Pacaguara-Mercier = Iñapari [inp]'; Pacaguara-Mercier is Glottolog dialect paca1247 under Iñapari (inap1242, Arawakan > Purus), whose md.ini lists 'Pacahuaras' as an altname and del Castillo as a source. Rivet & Tastevin (1919-20: 858) describe Mercier's 'Pakaguara' as a 25-word Arawak list (close to Piro/Ipurina) mistakenly labelled with the name of the Panoan Pacaguara (paca1246). The stress statement quoted is for modern Iñapari (inap1242, Peru; Rogers 2021, Parker 1995) and should be credited to inap1242, not entered as a separate paca1243 record; do not confuse with Panoan Pacahuara (paca1246).

sources.note: Iñapari word stress is lexically contrastive (anáʋa 'they' vs anaʋá 'canoe', háma 'to hear' vs hamá 'tapir') but overwhelmingly penultimate in elicited items; polar-question intonation shifts stress to the final syllable; some bound morphemes (causative -ʔá) carry fixed stress; a separate high tone is tied to certain morphemes.

sources.note: Iñapari is a 'restricted tone' / pitch accent language: each noun/adjective normally has one high tone, rarely on the first syllable except in some disyllables, all following syllables low; placement 'mayormente impredecible'; very few minimal pairs ([anáwa] 'ellos' vs [anawá] 'canoa'); all high tones written with an acute.
